articles.title: Grant Shapps blocked from standing again for the Conservatives
articles.summary: Kemi Badenoch tells the BBC she leads a "new party full of new people" as ex-MP is rejected as a candidate.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the BBC she leads "a brand new party full of new people" - after it emerged in the Spectator , external that the former cabinet minister and Tory party chairman Sir Grant Shapps has been rejected as a Conservative Party parliamentary candidate.

Sir Grant, who has declined to comment, served in nine ministerial roles in government as well as co-chairing the party.

In cabinet, he served as home secretary, defence secretary, transport secretary, business secretary, energy secretary and net zero secretary.

He was also a Foreign Office Minister, housing minister and international development minister , external .

He lost his Welwyn Hatfield seat to Labour's Andrew Lewin in 2024 by 3,799 votes after representing it since 2005.

But his application to stand again for the Conservatives at the next general election has been declined.

One party source told the BBC "it reflects badly on Kemi's temperament. North Korean purges don't work in British politics".

Badenoch told a news conference in central London: "We don't treat our former MPs or our candidates like tittle-tattle for Westminster gossip.

"What I will say is that we're going to be announcing candidates shortly, and you will see that this is a very different party from the one that was removed from government in 2024."

Asked repeatedly about her decision, Badenoch said that "commenting on individual applications would be absolutely wrong" but added that "I want people to know that this is a new Conservative party.

"It is not going to be making the mistakes of the past. We lost 250 MPs at the last election.

"We are changing policies, we are changing people, we are changing process. What I have said is we want people who are going to meet the standards which we are setting. Who are going to abide by the policies I have put red lines on. There could be all sorts of reasons for any individual to be allowed or not allowed on the list."

Badenoch has insisted that future Conservative candidates must agree to abandoning net zero carbon policies and to withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights.

It is not thought Sir Grant would disagree with either of these stances.

He also happens to be the co-chair of Conservatives Together , external , a group founded "to support and represent Conservative candidates."

He received a knighthood in Rishi Sunak's resignation honours list for "political and public service."

articles.title: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
articles.summary: The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, the BBC's political editor Chris Mason explains.
articles.body:
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England ; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills .

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No 10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of " the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen , external " and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that â he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead â both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.

She teased the new prime minister over his informal style â he "seems like a nice guyâ¦I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin.

"Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."

Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.

But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.

Firstly, on the domestic front â his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options â which criminals to free first.

Secondly, on the international front â after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again .

Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.

He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?

It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.

And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".

What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe.

Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.

Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?

And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?

Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister?

Given the intended long term home of No 10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032 , this is a live question.

Senior ministers and aides set to work from No 10 North Published 23 July

Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost? Published 20 July

Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost?

And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.

Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all â that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model".

It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one â where is your mandate for doing this?

The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction.

It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.

His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.

Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.

Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."

Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.

Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.

His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.

In other words, whether he is popular enough.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Democratic enthusiasm shapes North Carolina Senate race
articles.summary: Roy Cooper leads Michael Whatley by 9 points in North Carolina's Senate race, but an enthusiasm gap and Trump's favorability could reshape the contest.
articles.body: In North Carolina, more Democrats than Republicans say they are extremely interested in the midterm elections (51% vs. 42%), and more Democrats also say they are extremely motivated to vote (58% vs. 50%). This enthusiasm advantage creates an edge in the Senate matchup. Democrat Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by 53% to 44% in the race to fill the state’s open Senate seat, according to a Fox News poll of North Carolina voters. Cooper’s gap widens to 15 points among those saying they’re extremely interested in the election (57% vs. 42%) and 13 points among those extremely motivated to vote (55% vs. 42%). The race is unchanged among those saying they’re "certain" to vote (53% to 44%). FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS Whatley is the former chair of the Republican National Committee, while Cooper served as North Carolina’s governor from 2017-2025. The candidates are vying to fill the seat held by retiring Republican Senator Thom Tillis. Cooper receives high support from moderates, voters under age 30, independents, voters with a college degree, and women. He also captures support from about one in five non-MAGA Republicans and conservatives. Whatley performs best among very conservative voters, White evangelical Christians, White voters without a college degree, and rural voters. There’s also an enthusiasm gap when voters are asked why they back their candidate. Some 52% of Whatley’s supporters say they’re voting for him, while 46% say it’s mainly against Cooper. By contrast, 84% of Cooper supporters say they’re voting for him rather than against Whatley (13%). FOX NEWS POLL: SIGNIFICANT SUPPORT FOR BOTH VOTER ID LAWS AND MAIL-IN BALLOTS Most voters are committed to their choice: 81% of Cooper’s backers say they’re certain to vote for him and it’s 77% among Whatley supporters. Overall, one in five voters say they could switch their pick.  President Trump complicates the contest for Whatley. Forty percent of North Carolina voters view the president favorably and 58% unfavorable. That’s net negative by 18 points, while his ratings were underwater by just 6 points two years ago (47-53%). And Whatley’s ties to Trump concern 48% of voters, with worry extending across the spectrum, including more than half of moderates, more than 4 in 10 independents, and about 3 in 10 non-MAGA Republicans. Meanwhile, concern about Cooper’s ties to the Democratic establishment is more partisan. Overall, 42% are concerned, including 7 in 10 Republicans, but just 3 in 10 independents and moderates. "Recent data put the average Republican advantage in North Carolina statewide races at about 3 points," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the survey with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Cooper’s edge rests on almost unanimous Democratic support and commanding numbers among independents. To win, Whatley must stop the bleeding with non-MAGA Republicans and improve his standing with disaffected, less partisan Carolinians." Personal popularity also sets the candidates apart. Cooper’s 54% favorable rating is significantly higher than Whatley’s at 40%. In addition, Cooper is more popular than the Democratic Party by a 12-point margin, while Whatley trails the GOP by 4. Whatley is less well known overall, as 14% of voters say they’re unable to rate him or have never heard of him, including about 1 in 10 Republicans.  Tar Heel voters share equally negative views of the Republican Party (44% favorable vs. 54% unfavorable) and the Democratic Party (42% vs. 56%). Negative partisanship is strong, as more Democrats view the GOP negatively (94%) than view their own party positively (83%). The reverse is also true: more Republicans (92%) hold an unfavorable opinion of the Democratic Party than view the GOP positively (85%).  Among the small subgroup viewing both parties negatively, Cooper draws twice as much support as Whatley (64% to 32%). Inflation is the top issue for North Carolina voters, with 36% saying it will be most important to their vote for Senate. Next, it’s political divisions within the country at 14%, followed closely by healthcare and immigration at 13% each.  CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Half describe their financial situation as stable, 12% say they’re getting ahead, and 38% say they’re falling behind, which is 6 points lower than it was two years ago. North Carolina’s recent voting history points in different directions. Cooper won reelection in 2020 by almost 5 percentage points. In fact, Democrats have won 8 of the state’s last 10 gubernatorial elections. The last Republican to win was Pat McCrory, by about 11 points in 2012. At the same time, Republicans have won the state in 11 of the last 12 presidential elections. The last Democrat to carry the state was former President Obama, who won by 0.3% in 2008.  In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won North Carolina by 3 percentage points. Conducted July 23-27, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,005 North Carolina registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file.  Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (115) and cellphones (654) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (236). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ± 3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources used to develop weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population.  Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.  Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

articles.title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
articles.summary: The Green Party is grappling with how to manage its social media following a controversial post by its leader.
articles.body:
The Green Party of England and Wales is reviewing its social media operation which has been central to its surge in popularity over the past year, sources have told the BBC.

They insist it is not connected to the backlash to Zack Polanski this week after he re-posted a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel" - seen as being a reference to Nigel Farage.

But that incident has raised questions about whether it is sustainable for the Green Party leader to manage his own social media channels, with one party figure calling it an "avoidable mistake" and that Polanski "should have said sorry" for it.

In an interview with BBC Newsnight, Polanski repeatedly refused to apologise for "an inadvertent mistake" but acknowledged he needed to "be better on social media".

"I just didn't look carefully enough and I accepted it, as soon as I was aware of what happened I unaccepted it and took it down," he said.

Like other high profile figures on social media, Polanski receives a lot of material from other users seeking re-posts. But unlike most political leaders in the UK, he still manages his own accounts, rather than handing control to party staffers.

This may allow him to appear spontaneous and authentic - both valuable commodities on social media - but it comes with risks.

The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.

The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.

Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.

According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.

Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police.

Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action .

But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.

Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.

He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.

And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack.

One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.

They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".

It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.

They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.

Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.

But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".

She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."

But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".

Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.

It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.

One party source said there had been discussions among councillors and activists about whether Polanski was "too online".

"Is he just too online? Is he doing it all himself? Where's the professionalisation here, given the level the party's now grown to, and what people expect of us?" they said.

"There's got to be more checks and balances" the source added.

A separate party source confirmed there was a review going on internally into the party's social media operation, but would not be drawn on whether that meant changing who had oversight of Polanski's posts.

"We are looking at our processes and systems in this area," they said.

"Obviously Zack is really active on social media. It is how we have grown our reach and our membership."

Until around a year ago the party's entire social media team consisted of one full-time employee.

That has now gone up to three or four and may increase further following the review.

"We have expanded hugely as a party and we are looking at how we work," the source said.

"As part of that we are looking at what we might do to support and beef up our social media team."

They said the coverage of the Instagram re-post row had been "deeply irritating" but added that the review was not directly linked to that incident.

But it remains to be seen how much longer Polanski can retain control of his accounts before handing over the passwords to party staffers.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: GOP divisions shape Texas Senate race
articles.summary: Ken Paxton trails James Talarico by three points in the Texas Senate race as character concerns and a GOP unity gap reshape the 2026 midterm battle.
articles.body: President Donald Trump won the Lone Star state by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024, but a new Fox News Poll of Texas registered voters suggests this year's Senate race is far less settled. Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton has yet to fully unify the GOP despite the president’s endorsement in the GOP primary against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. In addition, more voters are concerned Paxton lacks the character to serve than worry Democratic challenger James Talarico is too extreme, and more Democrats than Republicans are extremely motivated to vote (by 7 points) and extremely interested in the midterms (by 6). Those dynamics give Talarico a 3-point edge over Paxton (51% vs. 48%) in the Senate contest (within the survey’s margin of sampling error). Talarico's advantage in the race grows to 6 points among both extremely motivated and extremely interested voters (53% vs. 47% in each group). FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC ENTHUSIASM SHAPES NORTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE Most independents (68%) and virtually all Democrats support Talarico (98%), while fewer Republicans are unified behind Paxton (89%). In part, that’s because one quarter of non-MAGA Republicans back Talarico (24%). Paxton is the choice among White evangelical Christians, White men without a college degree, rural voters, regular worship attenders, men and voters ages 65 and older. Some of Talarico’s best groups are Black voters, moderates, voters under age 30, Hispanic voters, women and voters with a college degree. "Although Paxton dominated Cornyn in the GOP primary, that bruising contest left scars," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson.  "He has considerable work to do with non-MAGA Republicans and independents, and that undoubtedly requires aggressively tying Talarico to the Democratic Party’s far left."  By a 12-point margin, more voters are concerned Paxton lacks the character to serve as a senator than believe Talarico is too extreme (59% vs. 47%). Twice as many Republicans are concerned about Paxton's character as Democrats are that Talarico is too extreme (36% vs. 17%). FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS Still, about 8 in 10 Paxton and Talarico supporters say their backing is more about where the candidates stand on the issues than who they are as people.  Trump received a 55% favorable vs. 44% unfavorable rating in the 2024 Texas Fox News Voter Analysis (FNVA) election survey. Today, those numbers have flipped: 45% favorable vs. 54% unfavorable, for a minus-9 net negative rating. Paxton garners a minus-6 net personal rating, 45% favorable vs. 51% unfavorable, while Talarico is in positive territory by 6 points, 49% vs. 43%. Talarico is more popular than the Democratic Party while the GOP edges out Paxton.  While both parties are viewed negatively, the GOP is underwater by only 2 points (48% favorable vs. 50% unfavorable), compared with the Democratic Party at minus-9 (45% vs. 54%). Despite Texas being a border state, nearly 4 in 10 say inflation will be the most important issue to their Senate vote, while 2 in 10 say immigration and 1 in 10 say healthcare, political divisions and unemployment. By more than a 2-to-1 margin, Texas voters say they are falling behind financially rather than getting ahead (35% vs. 16%). Half are holding steady. In the race for governor, incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is favored by 1 point over Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Part of Abbott's edge comes from a touch more crossover support: 12% of Talarico supporters back Abbott, while 9% of Paxton supporters back Hinojosa. Hinojosa has the advantage among extremely motivated (+6) and extremely interested voters (+5). Abbott has a net positive personal rating by a single point (50% favorable vs. 49% unfavorable). Hinojosa is in positive territory by 11 points (45% vs. 34%), although nearly 1 in 5 are unable to rate her. Texas last elected a Democratic governor in 1990 (Ann Richards), a Democratic Senator in 1988 (Lloyd Bentsen), and a Democratic presidential candidate in 1976 (Jimmy Carter). A closer look at the Hispanic electorate Hispanic voters say their Senate pick will be driven by inflation, as roughly 4 in 10 say it will be the most important issue to their vote and another 4 in 10 say they’re falling behind financially. This mostly matches views among all Texas voters. And as is the case with voters overall, there is an enthusiasm gap, as more Hispanic Democrats than Hispanic Republicans are interested and motivated to vote in the midterms. Overall, Hispanic voters prefer Talarico by 18 points (59% vs. 41%). Some 9% of Hispanic GOP voters crossover to support Talarico while 5% of Hispanic Democrats favor Paxton. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE In 2024, Trump topped former Vice President Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters in Texas by 1 point, according to the Texas FNVA survey (49% Harris vs. 50% Trump). By 20 points, more Hispanic voters are concerned that Paxton lacks the character to serve as senator than feel Talarico is too extreme (61% concerned vs. 41%). For the governor’s race, Hispanic voters back Hinojosa by 16 points in the new survey. By comparison, they preferred Beto O’Rourke over Abbott by 14 points in 2022. More than half of Hispanic voters view Talarico (57% favorable), Hinojosa (53%), and the Democratic Party (53%) positively, while more than half have negative views of Paxton (56% unfavorable), Abbott (56%), Trump (61%), and the Republican Party (59%). Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (72) and cellphones (681) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (253). articles.title: Colorado's socialist surge shakes up the Democratic establishment
articles.summary: A veteran Colorado political insider warned the democratic socialists' rise in Denver mirrors the MAGA movement and could become a cancer for Democrats.
articles.body: Democratic socialist candidate Melat Kiros shocked Colorado’s Democratic establishment when she defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the state's June primary. The double-digit win exposed a growing rift over the party's values that has left some Democrats stunned and questioning the future of the party. "If you had told me this woman would have won by 13 points, I would have bet my house against that," Doug Friednash, a veteran political strategist in Colorado, told Fox News Digital. "I never would have thought we would have seen a victory of that magnitude here in Denver." Friednash has tracked Colorado's political shift from red to deep blue over the past three decades, previously serving in the state legislature representing House District 10 in Denver. He later served as Denver city attorney and chief of staff to former Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper, and he currently works as a partner at Brownstein, a prominent legal and lobbying firm in the region. Kiros' victory was one of dozens of wins for far-left candidates in Democratic primary elections this cycle as socialists continue to ascend across the country. The far left's rise in the party has alarmed seasoned Democrats like Friednash. JEWISH COMMUNITY IN DENVER ON HIGH ALERT OVER RISE OF DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MELAT KIROS "It was one thing watching this happen in New York. ... But when it happens in a state like Colorado, which is really the gateway to the West, it tells me that this issue is going to spread and may be a cancer to the Democratic Party if they don't figure out what our values are," Friednash said. He noted that Kiros' victory did not happen in a vacuum, pointing out that DSA-backed candidates have successfully captured seats in the state legislature and city councils over the past few years. While Friednash originally predicted Rep. Diana DeGette would win, he acknowledged Kiros' campaign had a strong ground game and was able to tap into anti-establishment sentiments among progressives in the region. Kiros' team reportedly knocked on more than 100,000 voters' doors and ran a phone bank reaching 500,000 people leading up to election night. SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM She also campaigned on fighting for universal healthcare, affordable housing, utilities and more. Friednash said Kiros' message resonated with younger voters who are frustrated by the high cost of living and feel let down by the Democratic establishment. "I think the number one issue is affordability, by far," he said. "A lot of younger people that have moved to Denver have come here wanting to buy a house. They can't buy a home, it seems unaffordable and unattainable. And I think she's tapped into a lot of voter anger and hostility over things not being better." He believes Denver has become a microcosm of the national debate taking place within the Democratic Party over its future direction. Comparing the Democratic Socialists of America wave to the rise of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, Friednash warned that if party leadership refuses to call out the group's extreme policies, it will ultimately hurt Democrats in swing districts across the nation. RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN' "As I look out at what's happening within the Democratic Party, you know, it's kind of like a ship without a captain," Friednash said. "A lot of the more mainstream Democrats, rather than trying to say, 'Here are the issues we should be fighting about,' are embracing the socialists  because I think they're afraid of them ... much like I think we've seen with the MAGA movement. "While some Democrats may be falling in love with socialism, you know who isn't? The rest of America," he continued. "That dog's not gonna hunt in these more competitive primaries." Prominent centrist Democratic groups such as Third Way share that anxiety. The organization recently told The New York Times it plans to launch a $15 million campaign to combat the DSA movement, which it believes poses a "mortal danger" to Democrats and will hurt the party in potential presidential swing states. Concerns over the party's ideological turn aren't limited to establishment Democrats. Jon Caldara, president of the Denver-based free market think tank Independence Institute, also questions the future of his home state as democratic socialists continue to rise in prominence. "Without a doubt, the Democratic Party in Colorado has changed," Caldara told Fox News Digital, arguing the state has abandoned its historically pro-business stance. Caldara, a libertarian and longtime radio host and columnist, is outspoken about the challenges facing Denver and the broader state, such as affordability, homelessness and an exodus of businesses. He believes these issues will worsen, warning that establishment Democrats have lost control of their own party. "When the state started turning left, this machine was so powerful, it really couldn't stop itself," Caldara said. "And now it's really beginning to eat their own. It's kind of a French Revolution thing that you see that the Democratic Party here in Colorado is now well out over their skis. And there is a growing fight between Democrats and socialists. "The real telltale is that Democrats are afraid to speak the truth because they don't want to get canceled," he added. "It is vicious to go against the socialists." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' Caldara believes younger voters are increasingly being drawn to democratic socialist candidates in Denver and across the country because they lack historical context for how these types of policies have fared across the world. "Sadly, the young suffer from a terrible disease: It's called youth. And because they're young, they haven't seen failed socialism around the globe," Caldara said. "They haven't seen what happened in the Soviet Union. They haven't learned the lesson of Sweden, which looked like such a wonderful socialist paradise until it didn't work, and now they're turning into a capitalist system. They haven't seen this. "So, the idea that we can just redistribute rich guys' money sounds great," he continued. "We'll just do rent control. We'll do government funding. We all know how that's going to end up. It's going to end up poorly. And young people are going to be hurt. "I'm sad that they want to run this experiment again," he added. "And it's even sadder that it's happening in this beautiful free state, this western state, this pro-free-enterprise state of Colorado." Longtime Colorado residents like Gene Maine understand full well why socialist policies are appealing. But having fled the Soviet Union as a teenager in 1981, Maine sees unsettling parallels between the society he grew up in and the direction Denver is headed. As a child, Maine said he was often told that America, Western Europe and capitalism were evil. But as he got older, he realized the utopian society he was supposedly living in wasn't all that it was cracked up to be. REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER FAR-LEFT GROUP'S PUSH TO TRANSFORM AMERICA INTO 'CUBAN DICTATORSHIP' "As I grew older, I started recognizing that, ‘Oh my God, I'm being lied to. We're all being lied to," Maine recalled. "This is not the freest society in the world. It's a jail." After defecting from the USSR with his mother as a teenager, Maine lived in Los Angeles before settling in Erie, Colorado, in the 1990s, where he’s lived since, raising his family and working as an engineer. Over the past three decades, Maine has watched Denver change from a small "cow town" into a large municipality and witnessed a corresponding political shift as the population boomed. BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS "All of a sudden, it wasn't, 'Can we have the smallest government possible and leave us alone?' It became, 'Well, we need to give you free stuff.' And that's when I started to worry a little bit," Maine said. Maine isn't surprised that veteran Democrats are facing primary threats from the far left, noting that Kiros’ campaign benefited from a well-organized ground game and sweeping promises on healthcare and affordability that drew in younger voters. "She is winning the primary because we have an organized group convincing people that they can have free stuff. You can have free medical care. You can have free supermarkets. You can have free transportation. And it's very appealing," Maine explained. "I like free stuff, but what they forget to tell you is that nothing is really free. As they say, there's no free lunch." SOCIALIST HOUSE CANDIDATE SAYS HE AGREES WITH REPUBLICANS ON 'ONE ISSUE' He believes historical lessons are being lost as generations grow further removed from the realities of the Soviet Union. "So, there is a gap that's being exploited," he continued. "And it's been exploited from internal and from external, because there's a lot of evil forces in the world that do not want America to succeed." While critics view the rise of the DSA as a dangerous departure from American values, Kiros and other DSA candidates argue their policies are a pragmatic response to liberal voters fed up with how the Democratic Party has responded to their struggles. Kiros recently brushed aside concerns regarding communists inside the DSA faction of the Democratic Party, telling PBS "Firing Line" host Margaret Hoover there is room in the party for various viewpoints. "Yeah. Well, some members of the Democratic Party are proudly proclaiming themselves as capitalists, and it’s a big tent, right?" Kiros said. "But, again, at the end of the day, it’s up to the voters, right? "Until a self-proclaimed communist actually wins an election, then it’s just noise from the Republican Party. There’s no one who’s actually winning with that." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Kiros denied being a communist herself, arguing that younger voters are embracing the DSA message because, at its core, it represents "economic populism." Her campaign centered on Medicare for all, universal childcare, investments in public housing, higher federal taxes on the wealthy, publicly owned utilities and more. Like many other socialist campaigns across the country, she is also firmly anti-Israel.  Kiros' campaign was backed by several progressive groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party. Republican candidate Christy Peterson, a local accountant, is also running in the Nov. 3 general election, which Kiros is widely expected to win given the district's strongly blue lean. In 2024, Kamala Harris won 77% of the vote in the district en route to winning Colorado. articles.title: Discord suspenso pela ANPD: veja o que muda e riscos de bloqueio | G1
articles.standfirst: A ANPD suspendeu as transmissões ao vivo da plataforma por três dias úteis; entenda as próximas etapas da fiscalização e quando o Discord pode ser multado ou até bloqueado no Brasil.
articles.summary: A suspensão das lives do Discord pela ANPD busca proteger menores e pode resultar em multas de R$ 50 milhões ou no bloqueio judicial do aplicativo no Brasil.
articles.body:
A Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) determinou nesta quarta-feira (12) a suspensão das transmissões ao vivo do Discord no Brasil. A medida, porém, não significa que a plataforma foi suspensa no país : a decisão atinge apenas a ferramenta de lives .

LEIA TAMBÉM: Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados suspende transmissões ao vivo do Discord no Brasil

A determinação é preventiva e dá três dias úteis para que o Discord cumpra as exigências da agência. A suspensão vale até que a empresa comprove a adoção de medidas efetivas para proteger crianças e adolescentes .

Se as medidas determinadas pela ANPD não forem cumpridas, a agência poderá aplicar sanções administrativas como resultado da investigação.

Discord — Foto: Discord é uma plataforma de mensagens popular entre os jovens e jogadores de videogame — Foto: Ivan Radic/Flickr

De acordo com o Estatuto Digital da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA Digital), estão entre as possíveis punições a advertência e multas de até R$ 50 milhões por infração cometida .

A aplicação dessas sanções ocorre dentro do processo administrativo conduzido pela própria ANPD.

LEIA TAMBÉM: 'Panelas' no Discord escondem 'as mais perversas formas de crime' contra crianças, diz policial infiltrada

O ECA Digital também prevê sanções mais graves, como a suspensão e o bloqueio de aplicativos . Essas medidas, no entanto, não podem ser determinadas diretamente pela ANPD.

Caso entenda que uma suspensão ou bloqueio seja necessário, a agência precisaria pedir Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) que acione a Justiça. A decisão final sobre essas medidas caberia ao Poder Judiciário.

Por isso, a suspensão das transmissões ao vivo determinada nesta quarta-feira não equivale a um bloqueio do Discord no Brasil .

“O Discord não está sendo bloqueado. O que a medida preventiva suspende é a funcionalidade ‘Go Live’, utilizada para transmissões ao vivo em servidores fechados. O nosso objetivo é reduzir os riscos de danos graves ou de difícil reparação a que estão sendo expostas as crianças e adolescentes”, explicou Fabrício Lopes, superintendente de Fiscalização da ANPD.

Em nota, a plataforma informou que está analisando a determinação da ANPD e contestou a caracterização feita pela agência, dizendo que ela não reflete a plataforma nem os investimentos realizados em segurança. A empresa afirmou ainda que não tolera conteúdos que promovam ou incentivem a violência e que mantém equipes dedicadas a identificar e remover conteúdos que violem suas políticas. (Leia a íntegra abaixo).

A fiscalização ganhou força após a morte de uma adolescente de 13 anos no Mato Grosso do Sul. Segundo as investigações, a jovem teria sido induzida a atos de automutilação e ao suicídio durante transmissões em grupos no Discord.

O caso também levou o Ministério da Justiça a apontar falhas nos mecanismos de verificação de idade e de proteção de crianças e adolescentes da plataforma .

Na última semana, a primeira-dama Janja da Silva defendeu a retirada do Discord do ar no Brasil e afirmou que a medida deveria ocorrer “imediatamente”.

Na segunda-feira (10), o Discord apresentou à AGU uma proposta com medidas para reforçar a proteção de crianças e adolescentes na plataforma.

O documento foi entregue após reuniões entre representantes da empresa, do Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública, da AGU e da ANPD.

O governo havia cobrado mecanismos de verificação de idade, prevenção de riscos e proteção de usuários menores de idade.

Agora, a empresa terá de cumprir as determinações da ANPD para tentar encerrar a medida preventiva e evitar novas sanções no processo de fiscalização.

“Recebemos a determinação da ANPD e estamos cuidadosamente analisando seu conteúdo. A caracterização do Discord feita pela ANPD não reflete a plataforma que construímos nem os investimentos que temos feito na segurança dos usuários. O Discord não tolera grupos ou indivíduos que promovem ou incentivam a violência. Investigamos rapidamente e removemos o servidor privado, acessível somente por convite, envolvido no caso pouco depois de sua criação, e seguimos cooperando com as autoridades policiais na investigação. Além disso, nossa investigação encontrou evidências de que a atividade criminosa foi coordenada em outras plataformas antes da criação do servidor no Discord e continuou nessas plataformas após os indivíduos envolvidos terem sido banidos do Discord. Temos o compromisso com a segurança dos nossos usuários e contamos com equipes dedicadas em desarticular a atuação desses grupos, derrubar conteúdos que violem nossas políticas e tomar medidas contra os responsáveis por essas condutas em nossa plataforma. Esperamos continuar nossas conversas com formuladores de políticas públicas no Brasil para promover uma experiência online mais segura para todos os usuários, tanto no Discord quanto em toda a internet.”

articles.title: Under strain, Australia's world-leading disability support faces major restructure
articles.summary: The programme was game-changing for its users - but as costs balloon, its success has led to its downfall.
articles.body:
Annabelle Shaw is hockey-obsessed and on a winning streak, scoring eight goals this season for her team, the Panthers.

"I don't give up," she says proudly, adding that whenever she scores, she celebrates with a cartwheel.

And when Annabelle's not on the pitch, she's down at the gym. She likes nothing more than working out with her friends.

But Annabelle may soon have to stop playing her favourite sport.

The Year 8 student from Western Australia has Down Syndrome – a genetic condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 which leads to physical and intellectual disabilities. This enables her to access funding through one of the world's most progressive disability support programmes, the NDIS (National Disability Insurance Scheme).

Aimed at people with lifelong and severe disabilities, NDIS was created to ensure disabled Australians had greater independence and an improved quality of life.

Its design ushered in a very different approach to disability support – by providing people with funding based on their individual needs, and a certain amount of freedom to choose how to spend it. The scheme put disabled Australians and their families at the heart of the decision-making.

But the success of the scheme has also been its undoing – it's growing rapidly and costing the government too much. Now, under proposals introduced by the federal government earlier this year, tighter controls will be introduced to shrink its size and budget.

The money Annabelle receives is intended to help pay for therapies such as speech, as well as a support worker to help her on the hockey field.

"Annabelle needs somebody to break it down and say, okay, did you hear that, Annabelle? We've got to stand over here," says mum Gillian Croft, explaining the importance of a support worker for Annabelle at practice sessions, where there could be as many as 50 girls training at a time.

"Sometimes, especially if it's fast-paced, she disengages and she doesn't want to play because she doesn't understand what she needs to do."

The NDIS Amendment bill passed the House of Representatives at the beginning of July but was then delayed, extending a Senate inquiry into the changes at the same time. The report into that inquiry is due on 14 August. Shortly after, the legislation is expected to pass in the Senate.

The implications of the changes, say participants, could be huge.

Annabelle is one of more than 700,000 Australians who access NDIS funds.

The scheme was introduced under former Prime Minister Julia Gillard in 2012, although it took until 2020 for Australians across the country to be able to fully access its funds.

"Disability can affect any of us, from when you're born to a child's development, through the blink of an eye on a country road, through your genetic lottery as you age," Bill Shorten, Vice-Chancellor and President of the University of Canberra told the BBC. Shorten was instrumental in setting up the NDIS as then Parliamentary Secretary for Disabilities.

"What really makes disability hard is a lack of money and a lack of power," he explained, adding that the NDIS has enjoyed support from across the political spectrum.

When the NDIS started, it was estimated it would cost about $22bn a year, with about 475,000 participants. But this financial year it has ballooned to $54bn and the scheme now supports more than 700,000 people. Those figures are expected to keep growing, which is why the government is proposing a massive reset.

"It has grown too big too fast," says Hannah Orban, Senior Associate at the Grattan Institute and co-author of a report Saving the NDIS. According to her research, each of the participants receives an average of approximately A$65,000 ($44,800) of funding per year. Some, such as those with complex needs, receive considerably more; others receive far less.

"It costs a lot of money to run it and the government really does need to introduce good reforms to make it more sustainable so that it is here for generations to come," Orban says.

Before the NDIS, disability services differed across states. There was criticism that they were underfunded and inefficient. The NDIS brought in a game-changing new system but in doing so, all the other services that previously provided support fell away.

"Once we created the NDIS, there was a retreat from other disability services, so hospitals, schools - you name it - everything became an NDIS matter," says Shorten.

In 2024, changes were made to rein in ballooning costs – overseen by Shorten who had coincidentally returned as the Minister for NDIS. But that wasn't enough. Numbers kept growing. There's been a rapid increase, especially in the number of children accessing the scheme.

There's also been criticism that people are using the NDIS to access support not originally intended for the scheme, which was designed to address the needs of those with permanent or significant disabilities. According to a study by the Australian National University , there's been a 32% increase in the prevalence of autism since the NDIS was introduced. Experts, however, say the explanation for this is simple.

"People went into the NDIS because other systems were failing," says Jenny Karavolos of Australian Autism Alliance, who in June gave evidence at a parliamentary inquiry into the cuts. It may be that autism diagnoses have increased - but Karavolos argues that's because people need to access the right support. It is not, she believes, what's breaking the NDIS.

One of the other criticisms of the scheme has been that providers have gamed the system, offering unnecessary and expensive services.

"Where there's government money, there have been over-servicing and over-charging and shonky providers," says Shorten. "Many are good providers, but some are bad. That's the nature of a government scheme: people will hone in on it and try and slice off amounts for themselves."

According to the NDIS integrity chief, $3.7bn was handed out inappropriately in 2025 - a combination of misuse of funds and fraud. But tackling this won't solve the problem, according to experts.

"Fraud is low-hanging fruit," says Orban. "The government absolutely needs to tackle fraud and get on top of people who are rorting (cheating) this scheme because they're rorting people with disability and taxpayers, and it's just not acceptable. [But] the savings from fraud are really small compared to the other reforms that they've put forward."

Some of those include better cost control, tighter compliance, introducing more efficient assessments and moving children with lower support needs - those with developmental delays or autism, for example - away from early intervention provided by the NDIS and into a programme called Thriving Kids.

One of the most worrying aspects, say families and carers, is the plan to slash funding for social participation by up to 50%. That's the bit that people like Annabelle benefit from and that advocates say the NDIS was designed for: to enable disabled people to be an integral part of the economy and Australian society.

The government estimates that around a third of funding for people with Down Syndrome is spent on social funding. Without that, Annabelle's hockey playing would be at risk.

But it would impact disabled people more broadly too.

"It is a core goal of the NDIS to help people with disability participate in society and their communities," says Orban. "So it really doesn't make sense to be attacking this part of the scheme."

The proposals have prompted huge criticism of the government, which cites fraud and problems in the system but then proposes cuts to funding that is seen as central to creating independence for disabled people.

"This amendment is reckless, ill thought-out and entirely devoid of any shred of understanding of what living a disabled life is actually like for both the person themselves and their support network," said actor, author and disability advocate Hannah Diviney at the inquiry in June.

As somebody with cerebral palsy who needs a high level of support, she pointed out that she had been driven to Canberra to speak at the inquiry, and would be driven back – all possible because of NDIS funding.

"Any time I leave the house, if I am not with a friend or a parent, it costs something – that is an incontrovertible fact of my life," she told the inquiry. "Freedom, ambition, career, a social life – all of the things other people in this room take as a given, or as a right – has a price tag for someone like me."

While the NDIS budget is far bigger than expected, a large number of jobs have also been created to cater to the system, including physiotherapists, speech pathologists and support workers. And experts say that also needs to be considered while plans move forward to shrink it.

"I don't disagree that there needs to be reform about how the NDIS is operating - particularly how children are treated on the NDIS," says Darryl Steff, the CEO of Down Syndrome Australia. "All too often these cuts are seen in isolation and people are going, 'the NDIS costs us too much', but without acknowledging that every dollar spent in the NDIS contributes over two dollars to the broader economy."

In addition to job creation, NDIS support enables more disabled people to participate in the economy too.

"If Annabelle's playing mainstream hockey and she's out there with typical kids all the time and she's going to a mainstream school, that's her normal," Gillian says. "When she finishes school, she will expect to go and have a job and be in a workplace that's full of typical people."

With these proposed cuts, everything changes.

"She doesn't get exposed to any of that, and then we expect her suddenly to walk into the workforce without having any independence training all these years," Gillian says. "This is independence training for her, going to these sporting events and going to school, which in the end will be cheaper for government as well."

articles.title: Fox News Poll: New matchup, same result: Maine Senate race stays locked
articles.summary: Troy Jackson leads Susan Collins by two points in the latest poll, and Maine voters worry more about her Trump ties than Jackon's progressive links.
articles.body: Maine voters are weighing concerns about both U.S. Senate candidates, with anxieties over Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins' ties to President Donald Trump outpacing concerns about Democratic challenger Troy Jackson's progressive alignment, according to a Fox News statewide poll released Wednesday. Collins has represented Maine in the Senate since 1997, winning her fifth term in 2020 by nearly 9 percentage points.  The new survey shows more than half of Maine voters, 55%, are concerned her voting record aligns with President Trump too often, while fewer, 43%, are worried Jackson is too close to the democratic socialist movement. FOX NEWS POLL: GOP DIVISIONS SHAPE TEXAS SENATE RACE By a 14-point margin, more independents are worried Collins is too close to Trump than are concerned Jackson is too close to the democratic socialists.   Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from Allagash and former president of the Maine Senate, replaced Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee in July after Platner withdrew amid an assault allegation. Jackson’s candidacy makes the contest more of a referendum on Collins: 61% of his supporters say their vote is mainly against Collins, up from 48% when Platner was the opponent. Only 36% say they’re voting for Jackson, down from Platner’s 50%. FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC ENTHUSIASM SHAPES NORTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE The contrast is even clearer for Collins: 71% of her backers say they’re voting mainly for her, up from 53% in June. Just 27% are voting against Jackson, down from 45% when it was Platner. Despite a major change in the Democratic ticket, the survey finds the Maine Senate race remains competitive. Jackson tops Collins by 2 percentage points, 48-46%, well within the survey’s margin of sampling error. In June, Collins was ahead of Platner by 3 points. Since then, Collins’ support is down 4 points, while Jackson does 1 point better than Platner.  Among the subgroup of voters who rate themselves a 10-out-of-10 on certainty to vote, Jackson’s edge increases to 4 points (50-46%). By an 8-point margin, more of those backing Collins say their choice is locked in. One in five Jackson supporters say they may change their mind before voting. Roughly 9 in 10 partisans back their respective candidate, while independents narrowly prefer Jackson. Jackson’s best groups include liberals, women with a college degree and those under age 35. He also leads among men under age 45 and those in union households. He’s favored by women by 4 points, while men are evenly divided. Collins’ biggest support comes from conservatives, White evangelical Christians, men ages 45 and up and voters without a college degree. She’s also ahead among rural and married voters. Compared to Platner’s numbers in June, Jackson mostly holds steady with key constituencies including women, voters with a college degree and suburban voters, while making gains among those under age 45 (12 points better than Platner). At the same time, Collins’ previous 10-point advantage among men has evaporated.   Almost all MAGA Republicans back Collins, but that drops to three-quarters among non-MAGA Republicans (nearly one in five non-MAGA back Jackson). For Jackson, almost all supporters of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) movement back him, but that falls to two-thirds among non-DSA Democrats and independents. "Replacing Platner with Jackson has allowed two other factors to assert themselves — opposition to President Trump and a desire for change," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson.  "The race remains close, and I’d never count Collins out, but you have to give a slight edge to the Democrats here." FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT Collins is the only GOP senator running for re-election this year from a state Trump lost in 2024 (former Vice President Kamala Harris won the Pine Tree State by 7 points). Meanwhile, Trump’s personal favorable rating is underwater by 20 points (39% favorable vs. 59% unfavorable). Democrats view Maine as a must-win seat in their effort to take control of the Senate. Inflation remains the top issue in Maine, and one-third say it will be the most important factor in deciding their Senate vote. The other priorities are immigration/border security, healthcare and political divisions within the country. Part of Jackson’s lead is built on the support of the 4 in 10 who say they’re falling behind financially, where he leads by 29 points. Ratings of Collins are unfavorable by 10 points (44% vs. 54%), which is more negative than in June when her ratings were underwater by 3 points (47-50%). Jackson’s favorable rating is positive by a single point (47% favorable vs. 46% unfavorable). Views of both Senate candidates are more positive than those of their respective political parties.  Voters who hold negative opinions of both candidates prefer Jackson by 3 points in the horse race, while those viewing both major parties unfavorably back him by 22 points.  Ratings for both MAGA and DSA are about equally negative, with MAGA at minus 19 points and DSA at minus 21. However, there is more intensity in views of MAGA, as 50% have a "strongly" unfavorable opinion of it compared to 38% saying the same about DSA. Many more Democrats than Republicans say they’re extremely interested in the election (D+18), and are more motivated to vote (D+9), but nearly equal numbers of both groups say they are certain to cast a ballot in November (D+3).  In the governor’s race, Democrat Hannah Pingree continues to lead Republican Bobby Charles by 11 points, with third-party candidate Rick Bennett garnering 9%. However, nearly 3 voters in 10 say their preference in the race could change. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Party loyalty plays a big part in Pingree’s lead, as more Democrats (92%) support her than Republicans (83%) back Charles — and the largest share of independents favor her as well. Pingree’s personal favorable rating is net positive by 15 points (52% favorable vs. 37% unfavorable). Charles’ rating is underwater by 6 (36% vs. 42%), while 23% are unfamiliar with him. Bennett is even less well known, with 52% unable to rate him. Conducted August 6-10, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,000 Maine registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (128) and cellphones (626) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (246).  Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ± 3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.  Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

The nearly three-minute video features stylized graphics and shows locations where the younger Trump is publicly known to spend time. CNN’s Alayna Treene reports from the White House.

Escorted by Israeli soldiers, far-right Israeli lawmaker smashed a memorial in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank. The military says Sukkot violated the approved plan for the trip, but the firebrand politician had vowed one week before to destroy the memorial.

The Trump administration has quietly struck deportation deals with at least 35 nations, often worth millions, according to Third Country Deportation. Isobel Yeung investigates where the money is going and what happens to migrants sent to a country they’ve never been to.

Two fast-growing fires have hit North and Central Texas, with evacuations issued. No injuries have yet to be reported.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Economic anxiety and candidate concerns define Ohio Senate race
articles.summary: Inflation dominates Ohio voter priorities as 40% call it their top issue, fueling Sherrod Brown's 8-point lead over Jon Husted in the Senate race.
articles.body: Financial unease and voter concerns over Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted’s ties to the president are driving the dynamics in the Ohio Senate contest between Husted and former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. Brown seeks to regain his Senate seat by challenging Husted, who was appointed in 2025 after JD Vance became vice president. Brown narrowly lost his seat to Bernie Moreno in 2024. Underpinning the electorate’s mood is frustration with the cost of living. A new Fox News survey of Ohio registered voters finds inflation dominates their priorities, with 40% saying it is their top issue, far outranking healthcare, immigration, and political divisions. In 2020, 28% of Ohioans described their family’s financial situation as "falling behind." Now, that’s up to 38% — and those voters favor Brown by 40 points. Donald Trump won Ohio by 11 points in 2024. Still, a vulnerability for Husted is his connection to Trump, as 51% are concerned that he’s too close to the president. That’s up 5 points from 46% who felt that way about Husted in June. Plus, fewer voters, 44%, are worried Brown is too closely tied to the Democratic Party establishment. FOX NEWS POLL: NEW MATCHUP, SAME RESULT: MAINE SENATE RACE STAYS LOCKED These headwinds are directly fracturing party lines, with Republican defections to Brown undercutting Husted’s built-in advantage in a state where more voters identify as Republican than Democrat. While 87% of Republicans favor Husted, fully 97% of Democrats back Brown. The Democrat also draws 11% crossover support from Republicans overall and 25% among non-MAGA Republicans. Two-thirds of independents also favor Brown. All those factors help Brown remain 8 points ahead of Husted in the race for Ohio’s Senate seat, 53% to 45%, a margin unchanged since June. FOX NEWS POLL: GOP DIVISIONS SHAPE TEXAS SENATE RACE Brown’s lead expands to 10 points (54-44%) among those who rate their certainty to vote as a 10 out of 10, and to 15 points (57-42%) among those saying they are extremely motivated to vote. In addition, those most motivated to turn out this year — liberals, voters with a college degree, and supporters of the Democratic Socialists of America — prefer their former Senator. Brown has significant advantages among liberals (+88 points), urban voters (+37), those in union households (+31), voters under age 45 (+17), women (+16), and college graduates (+9). Husted is favored among conservatives (+65 points), White evangelical Christians (+42), White men without a college degree (+17), rural residents (+12), and married voters (+6). Meanwhile, Brown has the most positive personal rating of the candidates tested (51% favorable, 47% unfavorable), while ratings for Husted are 10 percentage points underwater (43% favorable, 53% unfavorable). Part of Brown's advantage is driven by affinity, as 67% of his supporters say their vote is mainly for him rather than in opposition to Husted. Among those favoring Husted, 58% say they are motivated to vote for him, not against Brown. Even so, the prospect of a shift is real, as one in five who are backing Brown and one in four supporting Husted say they could change their candidate preference before casting a ballot. Dissatisfaction with the party organizations and national figures is widespread. Majorities of Ohioans hold unfavorable views of the Democratic Party (57%) and the Republican Party (54%), as well as Trump (56%), the MAGA movement (57%), and the Democratic Socialists of America (54%). Views of Vance are divided, 47% favorable and 50% unfavorable. In the Ohio governor’s race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy receives 50% to Democrat Amy Acton’s 48%. That’s a small shift since June, when Acton was ahead by 1 point. Most supporters of both Acton (78%) and Ramaswamy (80%) have a high degree of certainty that they’ll stick with their candidate choice.  Fourteen percent of those favoring Brown in the Senate contest cross party lines to back Ramaswamy for governor, while 6% of Husted supporters prefer Acton, the Democrat. Views of Ramaswamy are divided: 46% favorable, 44% unfavorable, mostly unchanged since June. Forty-three percent have a favorable opinion of Acton, but her negative rating stands at 47%, up from 37% in June. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (78) and cellphones (694) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (236). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ± 3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. articles.title: Fox News Poll: A Senate battle looms in Michigan
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed trails Mike Rogers 51% to 47% in the Wolverine State Senate race, but Democrats show higher enthusiasm and engagement ahead of the fall.
articles.body: In Michigan, while more Democrats than Republicans are concerned about their candidates’ ideological views, Democrats are also more engaged and enthusiastic about the upcoming election, setting up a battle in the Wolverine State. After a heated Democratic primary, progressive Abdul El-Sayed secured the Senate nomination and will face Republican Mike Rogers this fall as Democrats try to retake the Senate. According to a Fox News survey of Michigan registered voters, Rogers has the edge in the race with 51% to El-Sayed’s 47%, within the survey’s margin of sampling error. FOX NEWS POLL: NEW MATCHUP, SAME RESULT: MAINE SENATE RACE STAYS LOCKED Rogers’ edge comes mostly from greater party unity among Republicans. Nearly all Republicans (96%), including both MAGA (99%) and non-MAGA Republicans (89%), back Rogers.  Only a week after winning the primary race, 9 in 10 Democrats (91%) and nearly all Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) supporters (98%) back El-Sayed, but that falls to 69% among non-DSA Democrats and independents. The small subgroup of independents narrowly favors Rogers. El-Sayed’s coalition includes liberal voters, Black voters, urban residents and women with a college degree. Rogers’ most loyal groups are conservatives, White evangelical Christians, rural voters and White men without a degree. Men favor Rogers by 11 points (44% El-Sayed vs. 55% Rogers), while women are split (49-48%).  President Donald Trump won the Wolverine State in 2016 and 2024, each time by less than 2 points, while former President Joe Biden won by nearly 3 points in 2020. El-Sayed is underperforming with Black voters, women and suburban voters compared with former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Rogers similarly trails Trump’s 2024 support among voters under age 30 and independents. That’s according to the 2024 Michigan Fox News Voter Analysis (FNVA). Voter enthusiasm for their candidate is evident on both sides. About three-quarters of each candidate’s supporters are certain they will stick with their choice this fall, and about two-thirds say their support is mainly for their candidate rather than against his opponent. FOX NEWS POLL: GOP DIVISIONS SHAPE TEXAS SENATE RACE El-Sayed leads among the most engaged voters with an 11-point advantage among those extremely interested in the election, a 7-point lead among those extremely motivated and a 4-point edge among definite voters (10-out-of-10 likelihood). Moreover, more Democrats than Republicans are extremely interested (+15 points), motivated to vote (+11) and certain they will cast a ballot this November (+7). More than half the electorate is concerned El-Sayed’s positions on the issues are too extreme (54%) and that Rogers is too close to Trump (51%). Voters on both sides of the aisle share concerns about their candidate’s ideological positioning. Twice as many Democrats are concerned El-Sayed is too extreme (30%) as Republicans are that Rogers is too close to Trump (14%). By a 10-point margin, more independents are concerned about Rogers’ ties to Trump than El-Sayed’s issue positions (58% vs. 48%). Trump’s favorable rating is underwater by 19 points in Michigan (40% favorable, 59% unfavorable). Both Senate candidates also have negative ratings, with El-Sayed (-13 points) faring worse than Rogers (-6). The two major political parties are viewed negatively. The Republican Party has a -12 net favorable rating while the Democratic Party is at -13. "The energy is on the left in Michigan, as it is throughout the country, and that should help with turnout," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson.  "But El-Sayed’s nomination path highlighted party rifts. He needs to reassure a wide range of Michigan Democrats — including Reagan Democrats, Jewish voters and Black voters — that he will serve their interests rather than pursue an extremist agenda." The MAGA movement is viewed more favorably than the DSA by 10 points (40% vs. 30%). However, more voters have strongly unfavorable views of MAGA than DSA (45% vs. 37%). Inflation is the top issue in the Michigan Senate race at 38%, and economic anxiety remains palpable, with 4 in 10 saying they are falling behind financially. Other voter priorities are immigration/border security and healthcare (14% each) and political divisions (11%). El-Sayed stays competitive thanks to voters who prioritize inflation (+10 points), healthcare (+47) and political divisions (+5), while most immigration voters prefer Rogers (+82). Those who say they are falling behind financially also back El-Sayed by 24 points. By an 11-point margin, Michiganders oppose the U.S. continuing to provide military aid to the Israeli government (44% favor vs. 55% oppose). Those favoring aid back Rogers by 45 points, while those opposed prefer El-Sayed by 29 points. Turning to the governor’s race … With Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer term-limited, Michigan’s gubernatorial seat is up for grabs. The Fox News poll finds Democrat Jocelyn Benson has the advantage over Republican John James by 5 points in the governor’s contest (52% vs. 47%). The results fall within the survey’s margin of sampling error. Compared with El-Sayed, Benson draws greater support among non-DSA Democrats and independents: 81% favor Benson in the governor’s race vs. 69% for El-Sayed in the Senate race. There is some ticket-splitting with Rogers’ backers nearly three times as likely to cross over for Benson as El-Sayed supporters are to back James (14% vs. 5%). Benson’s net personal favorable rating is +7 (49% favorable, 42% unfavorable), while James is at -3 (41% favorable, 44% unfavorable). articles.title: Discord: em quatro anos, ao menos sete operações policiais envolveram o uso da plataforma, diz Ministério da Justiça | G1
articles.standfirst: Plataforma tem até esta sexta-feira (14) para apresentar à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) informações sobre o que pretende fazer para tornar mais eficiente seus mecanismos de proteção.
articles.summary: Plataforma tem até esta sexta-feira (14) para apresentar à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) informações sobre o que pretende fazer para tornar mais eficiente seus mecanismos de proteção.
articles.body:
Entre 2023 e 2026, ao menos sete operações policiais envolveram o uso da plataforma Discord. É o que mostra documento do Ministério da Justiça (MJ).

"O CIBERLAB [do Ministério da Justiça] tem identificado, de forma recorrente, a utilização de servidores e comunidades hospedadas na plataforma Discord para compartilhamento e conteúdos relacionados a crueldade contra animais, automutilação, incitação ao suicídio, exposição de violência gráfica, disseminação de ideologias extremistas, cyberbullying organizado, coerção psicológica e transmissões ilícitas envolvendo vítimas vulneráveis, inclusive menores de idade", diz trecho do ofício do MJ.

Na última quarta-feira (12), a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) determinou a suspensão das transmissões ao vivo do Discord em todo território brasileiro .

A decisão foi tomada por meio de uma medida preventiva e estabeleceu o prazo de três dias úteis para que a plataforma cumpra a determinação.

Segundo a ANPD, a suspensão valerá até que o Discord comprove que adotou medidas efetivas para proteger crianças e adolescentes durante o uso da plataforma.

O Discord tem até esta sexta-feira (14) para apresentar à ANPD informações sobre o que pretende fazer para tornar mais eficiente os mecanismos de proteção da plataforma.

Suspensão do Discord: empresa chama decisão da ANPD de 'prematura' e diz que crimes foram coordenados fora da plataforma

Discord admite falha em sistema de alerta em live que vitimou menina de 13 anos

No documento, enviado ao Congresso Nacional há cerca de 15 dias, o MJ informou ainda que "conforme manifestação da Polícia Federal, há investigações em curso envolvendo o uso de plataformas digitais, inclusive o Discord, para a prática de diversos ilícitos, tais como crimes de ódio, indução à automutilação, exploração sexual, ciberbullying e outras condutas violentas, frequentemente envolvendo crianças e adolescentes tanto na condição de vítimas quanto de autores."

Em fevereiro, houve uma reunião entre o Ministério da Justiça e o Discord. De acordo com o ofício, embora a rede social tenha apresentado medidas na ocasião, "persistem desafios relevantes que demandam o aprofundamento de medidas preventivas e o fortalecimento de mecanismos de atuação proativa por parte das plataformas."

O Ministério da Justiça e o Discord foram procurados para comentar sobre o documento. Até o momento, não responderam.
