articles.title: Por que impacto da IA em eleições pode estar sendo exagerado, segundo pesquisador de Oxford | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo estudo desenvolvido por Felix Simon, IA tem poder muito menor de influenciar eleições do que se imaginava: 'a internet já está lotada de desinformação e embora seja possível criar mais, isso não significa um efeito maior'.
articles.summary: Segundo estudo desenvolvido por Felix Simon, IA tem poder muito menor de influenciar eleições do que se imaginava: 'a internet já está lotada de desinformação e embora seja possível criar mais, isso não significa um efeito maior'.
articles.body:
Durante os últimos anos, poucos temas despertaram tanta preocupação entre autoridades eleitorais, pesquisadores e empresas de tecnologia quanto o potencial da inteligência artificial generativa para distorcer eleições. A popularização de ferramentas capazes de criar áudios e imagens realistas alimentou previsões de que democracias ao redor do mundo enfrentariam uma avalanche de desinformação impulsionada pela IA.

Mas, para Felix Simon, pesquisador da Universidade de Oxford, no Reino Unido, as evidências disponíveis até agora sugerem que esse temor pode estar sendo superestimado.

'Para ser eficaz, seria necessário que houvesse algum tipo de demanda não atendida por mais desinformação, e isso não existe', aponta Felix Simon sobre conteúdos falsos gerados por IA durante eleições — Foto: Reprodução/Universidade de Oxford

Simon argumenta que a influência da IA sobre resultados eleitorais tem sido frequentemente exagerada e que fatores políticos tradicionais continuam sendo muito mais decisivos para moldar o comportamento dos eleitores do que, por exemplo, deepfakes divulgados nas redes sociais.

Em entrevista à BBC News Brasil, o pesquisador do Instituto Reuters para o Estudo do Jornalismo e do Instituto de Internet de Oxford afirma que a disputa pela atenção do público continua sendo uma das grandes limitações de qualquer estratégia de influência política, independentemente da tecnologia utilizada.

"O principal desafio para influenciar o voto das pessoas ou persuadi-las de uma forma ou de outra é conseguir que elas prestem atenção — e isso é muito, muito difícil", diz.

"O dia só tem 24 horas, e dessas passamos 8 dormindo e muitas outras trabalhando ou fazendo tarefas domésticas. No fim das contas, sobram mais ou menos 4 horas para entretenimento, interação com conteúdos e pessoas — ou seja, há uma competição gigantesca pela atenção durante esse tempo."

Além disso, argumenta, a grande parte dos conteúdos utilizados em campanhas nas redes sociais serve apenas para confirmar opiniões já formadas. Ou seja, quem tende a receber e consumir os vídeos, áudios ou imagens gerados por IA num contexto eleitoral são cidadãos que já escolheram seus candidatos e, muitas vezes, estão mais propensos a acreditar em notícias falsas que favoreçam seu viés.

"Para ser eficaz, seria necessário que houvesse algum tipo de demanda não atendida por mais desinformação, e isso não existe", aponta.

"A desinformação funciona porque existem pessoas receptivas a ela, geralmente pessoas que querem algo que confirme sua visão de mundo ou suas crenças sobre determinado partido ou candidato", diz o especialista.

"Mas a internet já está lotada de desinformação e embora seja possível criar mais, isso não significa um efeito maior."

Simon argumenta ainda que, embora os novos conteúdos criados com ferramentas avançadas de IA generativa sejam mais avançados e potencialmente mais persuasivos, os eleitores suscetíveis à sua influência não precisam ser convencidos de sua veracidade.

"Para os grupos mais suscetíveis [à desinformação], não são necessárias imagens muito sofisticadas", opina.

Um artigo publicado por Simon, ao lado do psicólogo e pesquisador da Universidade de Zurique, Sacha Altay, pela Universidade de Columbia, nos EUA, analisou ainda uma série de eleições realizadas entre 2023 e 2024, quando o temor em torno dos conteúdos gerados por IA já era grande. Mas segundo a pesquisa, os impactos previstos simplesmente não se materializaram na escala esperada.

Mesmo com a proliferação de ferramentas generativas, os resultados eleitorais continuaram sendo fortemente influenciados por fatores econômicos, culturais, sociais e partidários, além do papel desempenhado por líderes políticos e meios de comunicação tradicionais.

"A influência da IA ​​nas eleições nacionais foi amplamente ofuscada por outros fatores muito mais importantes, como a disposição dos políticos em desinformar, mentir e infringir outras normas", diz o artigo.

Os pesquisadores apontam também que os eleitores não chegam a uma campanha como folhas em branco, "apenas esperando para serem persuadidos". Em vez disso, os comportamentos de voto são moldados por um complexo conjunto de fatores, geralmente uma mistura de predisposições de longa data e fatores contextuais de curto prazo, dizem.

Estudos clássicos sugerem que a filiação partidária, muitas vezes formada já na adolescência, serve como um filtro primário através do qual os indivíduos processam informações políticas e votam. Elementos identitários — como vínculos com grupos sociais e orientações ideológicas — também interagem com os conteúdos e propagandas consumidas para moldar as impressões e os sentimentos dos eleitores em relação aos candidatos e aos temas políticos.

Em seu estudo, Simon e Altay apontam ainda que o fator humano deveria provocar mais temores do que a IA em si.

"Ao longo da história, os seres humanos demonstraram uma notável capacidade de inventar histórias falsas, desde lendas urbanas a teorias da conspiração. A desinformação sobre eleições é fácil de criar", afirmam.

Na entrevista à BBC Brasil, Felix Simon argumentou ainda que, em muitas ocasiões, a fonte da informação é mais relevante do que a qualidade ou o conteúdo das postagens.

Especialmente para os eleitores menos radicais ou extremistas, a avaliação das mensagens não tem como base apenas aquilo que eles veem ou ouvem, mas também a confiança em relação à fonte", diz.

"Mesmo que você consiga criar algo que seja mais convincente, isso não significa necessariamente que as pessoas simplesmente aceitem isso como verdade absoluta, porque temos vários mecanismos de vigilância epistêmica que, até certo ponto, nos protegem das informações falsas."

Outro ponto importante, aponta Felix Simon, é que as ferramentas de IA são facilmente acessíveis atualmente, o que significa que todos os lados da corrida política podem se beneficiar dos avanços tecnológicos proporcionados por elas.

Isso, diz, equilibra as forças e faz com que os efeitos práticos da IA em corridas eleitorais sejam menos visíveis.

"Não é apenas um lado que pode usar [a IA], o que cria uma espécie de corrida armamentista onde muito rapidamente se encontra um novo equilíbrio", diz. "Se um partido ou político começa a usar, seu adversário rapidamente aprende também e se adapta."

Nas redes sociais brasileiras, se multiplicam vídeos fabricados com inteligência artificial (IA) que usam a imagem do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que está atualmente em prisão domiciliar — Foto: Reprodução

Ampliação do nível de desconfiança e o futuro da IA na política

Tudo isso, porém, não significa que a IA seja inofensiva ou não possa causar estragos em eleições ou democracias, segundo Simon.

"Experimentos demonstram que, como esses sistemas são muito bons em criar argumentos concisos, estruturados e ricos em informações, eles são relativamente bons em persuadir as pessoas", aponta.

Além disso, diz Simon, a produção extensa de conteúdos gerados por inteligência artificial, assim como a própria discussão sobre o poder da desinformação no cotidiano atual, tem grande capacidade de provocar uma onda geral de descrença no sistema e nas fontes de informação.

"Se as pessoas sabem que os sistemas de IA são capazes de criar deepfakes muito convincentes, então, por padrão, algumas pessoas passam a duvidar até mesmo de conteúdos reais, pois não tem mais certeza no que confiar", afirma.

"Isso não significa que o mundo tenha perdido a confiança em todo tipo de informação visual ou oral, mas definitivamente significa que passamos a confiar menos nelas do que no passado."

O pesquisador argumenta ainda que a própria discussão sobre os perigos da desinformação e da IA para as democracias na imprensa e na Academia pode ampliar o nível de desconfiança da população.

"As pessoas podem passar a acreditar que a integridade das próprias eleições está comprometida ou que não se pode confiar mais no que se vê", diz.

"Isso, obviamente, coloca jornalistas e especialistas como eu em uma posição muito difícil, pois precisamos pesquisar e prestar atenção no tema, mas, ao mesmo tempo, não podemos exagerar nas afirmações, correndo o risco de produzir efeitos colaterais negativos", admite ainda.

Para o futuro, Simon acredita que o papel da IA em eleições ​​crescerá ainda mais "simplesmente por consequência da ampla disponibilidade e da crescente adoção dessa tecnologia".

Esse cenário, diz, não significa necessariamente efeitos negativos. Segundo o pesquisador de Oxford, cada vez mais partidos utilizam inteligência artificial para criação de materiais políticos e tarefas administrativas, o que contribui para sua eficiência.

"No fim das contas, uma campanha política nada mais é do que uma empresa", afirma.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: ONS planeja operação especial para acompanhar desempenho do sistema elétrico  | G1
articles.standfirst: Aneel comunicou ao TSE a antecipação de recursos destinados a usinas de produtores independentes que atendem áreas isoladas da Amazônia. O objetivo é reduzir o risco de desabastecimento nos dias do pleito.
articles.summary: Aneel comunicou ao TSE a antecipação de recursos destinados a usinas de produtores independentes que atendem áreas isoladas da Amazônia. O objetivo é reduzir o risco de desabastecimento nos dias do pleito.
articles.body:
Torres de transmissão de energia — Foto: REUTERS/Manon Cruz

O diretor-geral do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico ( ONS ), Márcio Rea, afirmou que, neste momento, não vê risco de falta de energia elétrica durante as eleições. Segundo ele, o órgão fará, como ocorre em grandes eventos, uma operação especial de acompanhamento do sistema.

“Sempre tem uma operação especial, mas a gente está trabalhando há meses, vem desenvolvendo (esse trabalho). Então, não vejo nenhum problema, a não ser que seja uma catástrofe”, afirmou Rea a jornalistas, em Brasília.

Em paralelo, o diretor-geral da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica ( Aneel ), Sandoval Feitosa, afirmou que comunicou ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) a antecipação de recursos destinados a usinas de produtores independentes que atendem áreas isoladas da Amazônia.

A medida busca reduzir o risco de desabastecimento de combustível para essas usinas em caso de dificuldades de navegação nos rios, provocadas pela baixa pluviosidade.

“Nós vamos antecipar recursos para que essas empresas comprem o combustível, deixem estocados, para, eventualmente, havendo algum problema no tráfego nos rios, haja combustível suficiente para atender as comunidades e, principalmente, durante as eleições”, afirmou Feitosa.

Os recursos são provenientes da Conta de Consumo de Combustíveis (CCC) .

Segundo Feitosa, a preparação para as eleições está sendo feita de forma preventiva. O objetivo é reforçar a segurança do sistema e garantir equipes suficientes para eventuais ocorrências.

“O que nós estamos fazendo, especificamente nesse caso, é trabalhar preventivamente. Quando estiver próximo das eleições, certamente o ONS vai tomar as precauções para deixar o sistema o mais robusto possível. Eles já fazem isso todos os anos, mas reforçaremos às distribuidoras a necessidade de reforçar as equipes”, afirmou.

Ao comentar as perspectivas para 2027, Rea avaliou que o cenário pode ser “complicado”, principalmente pela dificuldade de prever a intensidade e os efeitos do El Niño. “A gente entende que vai ser complicado, principalmente em 2027”, afirmou.

🔎 O El Niño é um fenômeno climático provocado pelo aquecimento anormal das águas superficiais do Oceano Pacífico Equatorial. Ele ocorre, em geral, a cada dois a sete anos e pode alterar os padrões de chuva e temperatura em várias partes do mundo. No Brasil, o fenômeno pode intensificar o calor, aumentar o risco de seca no Norte e no Nordeste e provocar chuvas acima da média no Sul.

Rea destacou, porém, que o sistema elétrico conta com medidas preventivas e alternativas para reduzir os impactos de eventos climáticos extremos. Segundo ele, ocorrências anteriores provocaram danos significativos à infraestrutura, mas não chegaram a interromper o fornecimento de energia.

“A gente tem um trabalho de prevenção. Não tem como saber o que vai vir, de onde vai vir o vento, mas, nos eventos que antecederam, conseguimos não ter interrupção de energia. Mesmo tendo mais de 20 torres afetadas, conseguimos manter o suprimento de energia”, disse.

Ele acrescentou que o sistema dispõe de alternativas para preservar o funcionamento da rede mesmo quando parte da infraestrutura é afetada.

“A gente tem alternativas nas nossas redes para manter o sistema sempre funcionando”, afirmou ele.

articles.title: New DC monument displays the names of 41 million veterans
articles.summary: The temporary monument will be up for visitors through Nov. 12, 2026.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A new monument on the National Mall is displaying the names of 41 million American veterans.

The National Military Monument, a temporary installation, will be on display through Nov. 12 to honor those who have served.

The one-of-a-kind monument features the names of more than 41 million service members, veterans and those who are currently serving, spanning across branches and generations alike.

Those names scroll through on the lines of the American flags, with two of them displayed on the National Mall. It takes days to go through all of the names.

Monument sponsor United States Automobile Association (USAA) told NewsNation that the response to the monument has been overwhelming for visitors.

“This was the first time for USAA to do something like this. We wanted to do something big for America 250, and just the feedback has been tremendous and overwhelming. You know, the lines of people hours long just to come pull up a loved one’s name or their own name on the monument and people told us they wanted it here longer,” said Christian Bove, USAA communications director. “So we listened and with the support of the National Park Service, we’re able to have this out here through November 12.”

The interactive nature is one of the unique features of the monument, with people on hand to help visitors search for a name and pull it up for display on the screen, allowing people to take photographs with the name of the veteran they are honoring.

articles.title: Burnham announces plans to clean up worst three illegal waste dumps
articles.summary: The government says the sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire contain 22,000 tonnes of waste.
articles.body:
Three of the country's worst illegal dumps are due to be cleaned up using taxpayers' money, the government has announced.

Sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire will be assessed for clearance, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying the "toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long".

Fines for waste offences will also rise from £300 to £5,000 to deter, catch, and punish those who dump illegally, and the Environment Agency will have more powers to seize assets bought with the proceeds of crime by those involved.

But opposition parties said illegal dumps were a small part of a much bigger issue with smaller scale fly-tipping and landfill all posing big problems for communities.

Burnham is looking to build on work started by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to tackle waste crime, with an action plan published in March detailing a series of measures - including using drones to map illegal waste sites.

Sir Keir's administration had announced that sites in Wigan, Sheffield and Lancashire would have government clean-ups - alongside Kidlington in Oxfordshire where removal of 20,000 tonnes of waste started in April .

The government said the new sites identified for clearance contain around 22,000 tonnes of illegally dumped waste.

They are: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road in Bradford, West Yorkshire.

West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester will be the first areas with new region-led approaches to waste crime.

The government said this will give mayors and council leaders the lead in co-ordinating councils, police, regulators, and other enforcement agencies.

Speaking on a visit to the waste dump in West Yorkshire, Burnham said: "We've begun a much more networked approach to this, where we're bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me."

The prime minister said the aim was to build intelligence about criminals linked to waste dumps at an earlier stage, to avoid the public being charged for clean-ups.

"We should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays," he added.

A new "waste crime crackdown group", chaired by Environment Secretary Angela Eagle, will bring regulators and law enforcement together in a bid to dismantle criminal operations.

Eagle said: "We are cleaning up sites, but we are also stopping the cycle, driving faster prevention and disruption, better intelligence, and stronger coordination across the system."

Hundreds of illegal waste tips operating in England - including 11 'super sites' Published 23 January

City sees more than 16 fly-tipping incidents a day

Kevin McKenna, Labour MP for Sittingbourne and Sheppey, one of the clean-up sites, welcomed the announcement, saying: "I want to see that momentum continue, with sites cleared, our environment protected and local people able to take pride in their community again."

A Green Party spokesperson agreed a crackdown was needed, but highlighted that smaller-scale dumping was a bigger issue and called for extra ring-fenced funding.

"We also need to boost the circular economy, so households and businesses are better able to reuse, repair, repurpose and recycle goods and make manufacturers and producers responsible for the safe disposal for the goods and packaging they produce," they added.

Liberal Democrat environment spokesperson Tim Farron welcomed tougher fines but said waste crime was only one part of a bigger problem, and called for an independent review of the waste system.

"Andy Burnham needs to wake up and smell the landfill," he said.

"New mayoral powers won't cut it if the National Crime Agency isn't empowered to clear these illegal sites, and stop legal sites spiralling out of control.

"We need an independent review of the whole system to crack down on these organised gangs once and for all."

The Conservatives and Reform UK have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: John Swinney defends £45,000 business-class flights to World Cup
articles.summary: The Scottish government spent almost £100,000 on official visits to the United States in June.
articles.body:
John Swinney has defended the use of more than £45,000 of public funds on business-class flights for him and two senior aides to the World Cup.

Scotland's first minister flew to Boston on 11 June for Scotland's opening match, before taking part in trade talks in Kentucky three days later.

While he and two senior officials travelled business class, Sports Minister Maree Todd and several other officials went to the US on significantly cheaper economy-class flights.

Swinney insisted the government had sought to "minimise" costs, while Justice Secretary Neil Gray defended the business class flights as a means of ensuring ministers "arrive fresh" when they travel overseas.

In total, the government spent £98,442 on trips for Swinney, Todd and their officials to the US, including flights, hotels and expenses.

Flights for Swinney and his private secretary John Webster cost £17,893 each.

Business-class tickets for the first minister's special adviser Colin McAllister cost £9,864.

The government spent a further £11,800 on economy-class flights for several officials accompanying Swinney, as well as more than £10,000 on car hire for the first minister's visit.

The cost of plane tickets for Todd and four accompanying officials to visit Miami for Scotland's final game was £5,485.

The Scottish government's travel rules , external state that business-class flights should only be used on flights of more than 10 hours "unless otherwise agreed".

Direct flights from Edinburgh to Boston typically last about seven hours.

Swinney told BBC Scotland News: "Obviously, when flights have got to be booked, when there's intense pressure on the time involved, then the costs are likely to be higher."

He added: "We tried to minimise those costs."

Earlier, Justice Secretary Neil Gray defended the use of business-class flights.

He told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast : "These are busy trips for ministers and it is right that they are able to arrive fresh, they're able to arrive in a way that means that they're able to participate and do their work immediately, so I think that's a proportionate use."

Gray pointed to benefits of the trip, such as increasing Scotland's "soft-power reach and the ability to make significant international connections".

He added: "It was right that the first minister and his team were there to participate and to be part of that."

Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn, speaking at the BBC's Scotcast live show at the Edinburgh Festival, also defended Swinney.

He said: "If we want our politicians to go and sit in row 46 beside the toilets and then land in Boston and then go and engage with US government officials having done so we'll get exactly what we deserve as politicians."

Releasing the travel expenses, the government said the US trips were made to support the national team at the World Cup as well as to hold talks on trade, tourism, culture and investment.

Conservative MSP Stephen Kerr said: "Nobody begrudged SNP ministers joining the Tartan Army to cheer on Scotland men's team at their first World Cup appearance in nearly three decades, but in typical SNP fashion costs were never kept under control.

"Swinney and his ministerial colleague were clearly happy to escape all the challenges facing them back home, but they should have met these significant costs out of their own pocket."

articles.title: Young Democrats eye Congress with affordability at the top of their agenda
articles.summary: A new generation of young progressive Democrats could enter Congress next year with a deeply personal connection to the economic issues at the center of their campaigns — and a desire to make those policy items a bigger part of the party’s agenda. For many of these potential lawmakers, the inability to afford a house…
articles.body:
A new generation of young progressive Democrats could enter Congress next year with a deeply personal connection to the economic issues at the center of their campaigns — and a desire to make those policy items a bigger part of the party’s agenda.

For many of these potential lawmakers, the inability to afford a house and rising healthcare costs are some of the top issues that have shaped their lives and those of their peers. That firsthand experience, they argue, has given younger Democrats a different sense of urgency around challenges that have become increasingly difficult for their generation to navigate.

“I am a millennial. Many of the colleagues that are running right now and being elected across the country right now are millennials,” said 36-year-old Claire Valdez, the Democratic nominee running to represent New York’s 7th Congressional District.

“We have seen our futures foreclosed upon us. You know, we can’t imagine having children or buying houses or retiring in the future, and that’s a kind of like frustration and dissatisfaction among young people all over the country that needs to be heard — that needs to be heard in the halls of power,” she added.

But that mandate could run up against the realities of Congress, where seniority, relationships and institutional knowledge still carry considerable weight.

That could create an early test for both the incoming lawmakers and Democratic leadership: Younger members will have to learn to navigate an institution where policy expertise and procedural rules matter, while party leaders will have to decide how much influence to give a new generation eager to make its mark.

“I think the younger members are going to come in and try to change Congress, and the older members are going to have the perspective of come in and do not let the Congress change you,” said Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright. “And … I think perspective, patience are going to be the two — and process — are going to be the three critical things. I think that in this environment, they’re going to have to learn that you need 218, 217 other people to agree with you in order to move a piece of legislation.”

The push for generational change has been reflected in a string of Democratic primary victories by younger candidates in recent weeks. This includes 32-year-old Darializa Avila Chevalier defeating Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.) in New York’s 13th Congressional District primary, 31-year-old Angela Gonzales-Torres winning the Democratic nomination in California’s 34th Congressional District and 29-year-old Melat Kiros ousting 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.) in Colorado’s 1st Congressional District primary, among others.

Like Valdez, these candidates have shown little hesitation in making the high cost of living a key part of their campaigns, arguing that Washington has done very little to address the issue. Some of the policies they’ve advocated for include universal healthcare and childcare, stronger worker protections, fair wages and expanded housing vouchers.

Asked how aggressively she thinks Democrats should stand up to the Trump administration on these issues, Valdez said, “I think we need to be as aggressive as possible.”

“We need to be using every single tool in our toolbox, even if we don’t have, you know, a Democratic trifecta. We need to be demonstrating to our constituents, the American public, that we are fighting back, and we’re setting ourselves up for, you know, in a couple of years when you know, hopefully we have a Democratic president, and we can start moving a lot of the priorities forward that will actually transform American life,” she said.

But that push for a more aggressive approach could clash with moderate and senior members of the caucus, who have greater experience navigating the legislative process and may favor a more measured strategy aimed at winning Republican support and avoiding an overly partisan path forward.

Even so, Rep. Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), 71, said he expects young progressive Democrats, moderates and senior members of the caucus to find common ground on a range of issues, including affordability. He said he’s got a bill to regulate the price of all drugs that he hopes incoming first-term lawmakers will co-sponsor.

“I’m a member of both the progressive and the new Dems, and I think new Dems want to bring prices down. I think progressives want to bring prices down, and I think the whole country wants us to bring prices down. So, whether it’s allowing Americans to pay an awful lot less at the pump because we produce more oil than we consume, or whether it’s to have Americans pay European prices for pharmaceuticals, there’s a lot we could do to lower prices,” Sherman argued.

He added that he thinks if Democrats win back the House, they will likely operate on a razor-thin margin.

“The one thing they have to do is learn to passionately disagree in the private caucus meeting and then come out and vote as a unified bloc on the floor of the House,” Sherman said.

“That’s something Democrats didn’t have to learn in 2024 because we’re not in the majority. Although even then we have been, you know, even the minority has a reason to — we have voted with a level of loyalty and consistency that is way beyond what I saw 20 years ago. So I think … the views we express privately may be diverse. Even the views we express to the press may be diverse. But our votes have got to be unified,” he added.

Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.), 81, said there will always be standout first-term lawmakers who bring charisma and quickly rise through the ranks, earning the attention of the broader Democratic caucus. He added that incorporating the voices of those emerging leaders and the ideas they bring to the table will be key next year if Democrats win back the majority.

“I’m glad we have new people, and some of them are going to, you know, probably not want to wait. You know, they may want to just step right in on the first day and, you know, want to take some leadership, and I think we have to be very, very understanding of their impatience and not put it down,” Cleaver said.

articles.title: Rubio outperforms Vance in hypothetical 2028 match-ups: Poll
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio performed slightly better than Vice President Vance in multiple hypothetical 2028 presidential match-ups against Democratic candidates, according to a new poll. The Emerson College and The Hill survey found that in five match-ups against Democrats, Rubio outperformed Vance in all but one — with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg holding…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio performed slightly better than Vice President Vance in multiple hypothetical 2028 presidential match-ups against Democratic candidates, according to a new poll.

The Emerson College and The Hill survey found that in five match-ups against Democrats, Rubio outperformed Vance in all but one — with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg holding a 5-point edge against both Republicans.

While Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) and California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) both had 5-point leads over Vance, their leads over Rubio were 3 and 2 points, respectively.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, meanwhile, led Vance with 49 percent support to his 45 percent. But Rubio flipped the script and led Harris by 5 points.

Progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) trailed Vance by 2 points and Rubio by 5 points. Ocasio-Cortez was the only candidate to lose to both Republicans.

At least 6 percent of the 1,000 respondents were undecided in every match-up, with 11 percent undecided in a hypothetical bout between Vance and Ocasio-Cortez.

The Emerson College and The Hill survey had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

Neither Vance nor Rubio has said publicly whether they will run for president in 2028 , although they are the consensus top two in recent polls of likely GOP voters .

The secretary of State, who finished third in the 2016 GOP primary behind President Trump and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), told Vanity Fair last year he will defer to the vice president if he seeks the GOP nomination.

Vance said in June he will discuss a presidential run with his wife, second lady Usha Vance, after the November midterms. Usha Vance gave birth in July to the couple’s fourth child.

“The way I make decisions is, I try not to make them until I absolutely must,” the vice president told Robert Costa on “ CBS Sunday Morning .”

The 2028 GOP primary will be the first without Trump on the ballot since 2012. While the president has not weighed in publicly on his preference between Vance and Rubio, The Washington Post reported earlier this month he recently told donors in the Oval Office, “At the end of the day, we need to elect JD.”

In response to that report, Trump said while Vance is “great,” it is “way too early to even be thinking about that.”

The president has also mentioned a potential Vance-Rubio ticket for 2028. In June, he said the populist Vance and the traditionally conservative Rubio would make “a great team.”

“I don’t know how you beat them if they’re together,” he told Miranda Devine on an episode of the New York Post’s “ Pod Force One .”

articles.title: GOP trails Democrats by 8 points on congressional ballot in new poll
articles.summary: Republicans are trailing Democrats by about 8 points on a generic congressional ballot, according to a new poll from Emerson College and The Hill. In the survey, 50.7 percent of respondents said they would back a Democrat if the midterm elections were held that day, and 43 percent said they would back a Republican, with…
articles.body:
Republicans are trailing Democrats by about 8 points on a generic congressional ballot, according to a new poll from Emerson College and The Hill.

In the survey, 50.7 percent of respondents said they would back a Democrat if the midterm elections were held that day, and 43 percent said they would back a Republican, with 6.3 percent unsure.

Democrats would need to flip four Senate seats and net four House seats to clinch control of Congress.

The poll comes amid rocky political territory for the GOP as they head into this year’s midterms. Republicans are facing President Trump’s slumping approval rating, an unpopular Iran war and concerns about the economy.

The economy remains the top issue among voters, according to the Thursday poll. Meanwhile, opposition to the war in Iran has increased by 2 points while support for the operation has decreased by 4 points.

Trump’s approval rating has remained steady at around 40 percent in Emerson polling since April. According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was 40.4 percent on Wednesday afternoon, with his disapproval rating at 56.3 percent .

Earlier this month, the president told Punchbowl News that voters are “angry” at congressional Republicans — not him. Still, some Republicans see Trump as a growing liability ahead of the midterms.

On Wednesday, former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) said he was “worried” about the GOP’s chances of holding onto control of Congress in the wake of the midterms.

“I’m worried that I’m not seeing the clear message from Republicans, what is the plan of why you should stay in the majority?” McCarthy told Fox News’s Dana Perino.

The former Speaker questioned what Republicans’ economic plan is going into next year and what the party’s latest victories have been as examples. He said that some states’ elections worried him.

The Emerson College/The Hill poll took place from Aug. 16 to 17, featuring 1,000 likely voters and 3 percentage points as its credibility interval.

articles.title: The Memo: Angie Nixon’s shock Florida win gives fresh boost — and a new test — for the left
articles.summary: The left of the Democratic Party scored its biggest upset of the year on Tuesday — and it did so in Florida, a state that is usually inhospitable territory for anything adjacent to socialism. State Rep. Angie Nixon (D) beat Alex Vindman handily in the Democrats’ U.S. Senate primary. Nixon, a progressive lawmaker and organizer…
articles.body:
The left of the Democratic Party scored its biggest upset of the year on Tuesday — and it did so in Florida, a state that is usually inhospitable territory for anything adjacent to socialism.

State Rep. Angie Nixon (D) beat Alex Vindman handily in the Democrats’ U.S. Senate primary.

Nixon, a progressive lawmaker and organizer who recently joined the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), beat Vindman by more than 12 points, despite suffering from a 16-to-1 fundraising disadvantage.

Nixon found success running largely on economic issues. She supports “Medicare for All,” free childcare and a significant increase in the minimum wage. Notably, those are all policies that poll strongly among Democrats — and, by and large, among the broader population.

Vindman had been best known as a central witness in President Trump’s first impeachment. On Wednesday, Trump gloated about Vindman’s defeat (“the most gratifying loss last night”) while also deriding Nixon’s chances in the general election.

She is, the president insisted, “a Radical Left Lunatic” who would “go down to certain defeat” in November against Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.). Moody was appointed to the Senate by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) as a replacement for Marco Rubio, who left the upper chamber to become Trump’s secretary of State.

Democrats, naturally, don’t see Nixon either as a “lunatic” or as one who is doomed to defeat. But they do acknowledge that she will have an uphill climb to win the general election, even at a time when Trump’s approval ratings are bumping around close to all-time lows.

Florida, having been a key battleground for years, has become safer Republican territory. No Democrat has carried it at the presidential level since former President Obama. Rubio won his 2022 reelection for the Senate by 16 points, and Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) won reelection two years later by 13 points.

Steve Schale, a Democratic strategist who was the Florida state director in Obama’s 2008 victory, said that either Nixon or Vindman would face a “tough path” to get to 50 percent in November.

Asked if he believed the gradient was even steeper for Nixon, Schale said he could argue the case either way.

The pro-Nixon argument, he said, is that she has the capacity to energize voters, especially young progressives and the African American community.

Notably, Nixon was victorious in Tuesday’s primary in low-income areas and in areas with large Black populations — a rebuke of sorts to those who argue that the current leftist energy is largely confined to affluent, young white people.

On the other hand, Schale noted, Nixon faces real obstacles in the increasingly Republican state. The basic partisan math, he said, requires Democratic candidates to peel off a significant number of voters who normally back the GOP if they are to have any real chance of victory.

“The challenge for Angie is: Who are those voters that voted for Trump and voted for Rubio and are going to vote for Republican state legislators who are also going to vote for Angie Nixon?” he said.

Defenders of Nixon note that her focus on economic issues plainly resonated at least in the primary. They say she should not be underestimated in the general election.

Some also note that Florida’s increasingly red hue can obscure some of its political complexity. For example, in 2020, Trump carried the state even while losing the national election to former President Biden. Yet, on the same day, Florida voters overwhelmingly passed an amendment increasing the minimum wage.

Nixon is seeking to capitalize on economic discontent and broad antiestablishment sentiment much more than an on ardor for abstract socialist ideals.

In a TikTok video back in January, she cast herself as a fighter for working Americans who have suffered under the status quo.

“Florida, we have a problem: Corrupt politicians in D.C. are working for greedy corporations instead of fighting for the rest of us,” Nixon began. “Enough is enough. Something has to change.”

That’s the kind of message that has plainly resonated in other Democratic primaries this year, as incumbents have fallen to leftist challengers from New York to Colorado.

Florida Democratic strategist Jackson McMillan was one of the few to argue before Tuesday’s primary that Nixon had a real chance of winning. He told this column that the media focus on DSA was somewhat beside the point — especially given how recently Nixon had affiliated herself with the organization.

Speaking of her rise and that of similar candidates elsewhere, McMillan said, “It gets a lot of clicks to say ‘The rise of DSA,’ but I think they are mostly just offering solutions that the Democrats refuse to commit to.”

McMillan cited Medicare for All as one example, describing himself as “a capitalist” and business owner who is frustrated by the high cost of medical insurance for himself and his employees. Politically, he see the appeal of candidates like Nixon as having less to do with doctrinaire socialism than with a reaction against corporations and other monied interests “failing to honor the social contract.”

Others in the party, however, note the particular challenges for candidates on the left in Florida.

The state is home to sizable communities of Cuban Americans, Venezuelan Americans and Nicaraguan Americans, many of whose family histories are characterized by memories of personal suffering at the hands of Marxist-inspired “strongmen.”

Fernand Amandi, a Democratic pollster in Florida who is Cuban American, was asked about the difficulties in the state for explicitly socialist candidates.

“It’s not ‘difficult,’” he responded. “It’s a nonstarter.”

But Amandi argued that Nixon doesn’t fit so easily in the DSA box because of her history outside of the group, her lengthy record as an organizer and the trust she has built up with many Democratic voters over years.

“I don’t think there’s an appetite for the DSA in Florida — or socialism,” he said. “But having said that, Angie Nixon is a longtime party stalwart who is a talented campaigner and who centered her message around the cost of living and economic concerns. Those are by far the biggest issues in Florida.”

To be sure, victory in Florida may ultimately prove beyond Nixon.

But, if that is the outcome, it will be harder for centrists to say she has lost a race a more moderate Democrat would have won. Florida is very different in its political complexion from Michigan, where Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed offers a tidy test case of whether leftist candidates can win in battleground states.

For all the challenges, Nixon is talking up her chances.

“I’ve unseated incumbents before. I’ve been outspent 5-to-1,” she told MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday. “Ashley Moody will be calling me ‘senator’ in November.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Trump reveals exact number of North Korea's nuclear weapons
articles.summary: Trump cited 57 nuclear weapons in North Korea's arsenal, marking the first time a U.S. official has publicly put an exact number on Pyongyang's stockpile.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Wednesday that North Korea possesses 57 nuclear weapons as he previewed a possible meeting with leader Kim Jong Un later this year. Trump made the remark while defending his relationship with Kim, arguing that his rapport with the North Korean leader is "a good thing," not a bad one. Trump’s unusually precise figure appears to be the first time a U.S. official has publicly put an exact number on North Korea’s nuclear arsenal. Public assessments have generally estimated that Pyongyang has roughly 50 to 60 assembled warheads, while warning that the country’s secretive program makes a definitive count impossible. It was not immediately clear whether Trump’s specific figure was based on a classified U.S. intelligence assessment. TRUMP ORDERS MAJOR CUT TO US-SOUTH KOREA DRILLS AS NORTH KOREA RAMPS UP MISSILE TESTS Trump said Kim is "a very powerful player" and blamed prior administrations for allowing North Korea to develop a nuclear arsenal. "The fact that I get along with him, that’s a good thing," Trump said. "You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon. And I know Kim Jong Un very well, and he’s going to be fine as long as we have a smart president." Trump said he expected to meet with Kim later this year, though he did not provide a date or location. NORTH KOREA EXPERT WARNS US CAN 'NEVER TAKE THEIR EYE OFF' KIM JONG UN FOLLOWING MISSILE TEST DURING IRAN WAR North Korea’s nuclear stockpile is closely guarded, and public estimates vary. The Federation of American Scientists estimated in 2024 that Pyongyang may have assembled roughly 50 nuclear warheads, while possessing enough fissile material for up to 90. Trump’s comment came after he ordered War Secretary Pete Hegseth this week to substantially scale back the annual U.S.-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, arguing that the drills were costly and sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea. The U.S. and South Korean militaries said Wednesday they would shorten the exercises and end them Friday. The decision is one of several overtures Trump has made toward Kim as he seeks to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Trump has said he expects to meet with Kim later this year, potentially during a planned November trip to Asia, though no summit has been announced. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, dismissed the reduction in drills as insufficient, saying Washington’s policy toward North Korea remains hostile. Trump and Kim met three times during Trump’s first term, but their negotiations broke down in 2019 without an agreement to curb North Korea’s nuclear program. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP North Korea’s arsenal remains far smaller than those of the world’s two largest nuclear powers. Russia has about 4,400 nuclear warheads in its military stockpile, while the United States has 3,700, according to January estimates by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. China has 620, followed by France with 290, the United Kingdom with 225, India with 190, Pakistan with 170 and Israel with 90. SIPRI estimated North Korea has about 60 assembled warheads — broadly in line with Trump’s figure — while cautioning that the secrecy surrounding Pyongyang’s program makes precise counts uncertain.
